name: Keoru-Ahia
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Only one-page wordlists in Glottolog (Franklin 1973, colonial lists); no grammar or phonology known.

new_statements.quote: Stress. In both Orokolo and Toaripi, with words of two or three syllables, the stress is normally on the penultimate syllable. There are some exceptions, the most notable being with the nominative form of the personal pronouns: ara /ará/ 'I', are /aré/ 'he', 'she', 'it'; ere /eré/ 'they'. The stress pattern here has possibly been influenced by the object and genitive markers, the addition of which to a pronoun normalises the stress. ... With words of four or more syllables, the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress has a minor stress, e.g. karikara /kàrikára/ 'village'. The stress of the stem is repeated in reduplicated words, e.g. hirihiri /hírihíri/ 'dirty'.
new_statements.citation: Brown, Herbert A. 1986. A comparative dictionary of Orokolo, Gulf of Papua. Pacific Linguistics C-84. Canberra: Australian National University. (Introduction, section 'Stress'.) Corroborated by Brown, H.A. 1973. The Eleman language family. PL C-26: p.307 (Toaripi stress rule) and p.350 ('In stress, juncture, and intonation Orokolo is in agreement with Toaripi').
new_statements.locator: p. xiv, Introduction, section 'Stress' (PDF page 14 of the sealang file)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (stated for Orokolo and Toaripi); a final diphthong counts as two syllables (Brown 1973 p.307); nominative personal pronouns are exceptionally final-stressed, reverting to penultimate when suffixed with -ro/-ve.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In words of four or more syllables a minor stress falls two syllables before the penultimate main stress (i.e. alternating leftward: kàrikára); reduplicated words carry the stem stress on each copy.
new_statements.exceptions: Nominative personal pronouns ara, are, ere (final stress); Brown 1973 p.307 adds Toaripi faitora /fáitora/ 'now', havou, pitoo with final stress, and onomatopoeic words reversing the pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule from citation forms; Brown 1973 pp.307-308 adds that noun+modifier and noun+postposition form one phonological word with main stress on the modifier/postposition, and that phrase intonation puts the accent on the last major stressed syllable. IMPORTANT: the statement is made for Orokolo (orok1267) and Toaripi (toar1246), not for Keuru/Ahia by name; Brown treats Keuru-Belepa (Haura Haela) and Aheave as Western Eleman dialects with 'close affinity with Orokolo' (1973 p.296) and includes KR/HH forms in the 1986 dictionary, but never states their stress separately.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted stress statement is for Orokolo (orok1267) and Toaripi (toar1246), the two Eleman languages H.A. Brown described first-hand. Keoru-Ahia (xeu) corresponds to Brown's Western Eleman dialects 'Keuru (Belepa)' = Hae Haela + Haura Haela (Glottolog alt names Keuru, Belepa, Haura Haela) and 'Aheave' (= Ahia, on the Vailala River); Brown 1973 (Table 3, pp.295-296) lists them beside Orokolo and Opao as separate Western Eleman dialects with 'close affinity with Orokolo', and Brown 1986 cites Keuru (KR) and Haura Haela (HH) forms inside the Orokolo dictionary. No source states stress for Keuru or Ahia by name; applying the penultimate rule to keor1235 is an inference from the closest described relative, not a first-hand statement about this glottocode.

sources.note: Introduction p.xiv, section 'Stress': in both Orokolo and Toaripi words of two or three syllables normally have penultimate stress; nominative personal pronouns (ara, are, ere) are final-stressed; in words of four or more syllables the syllable two before the penult carries a minor stress; reduplications repeat the stem stress. The dictionary cites Keuru (KR) and Haura Haela (HH) dialect forms (abbreviations p.xxi) but the stress statement is scoped to Orokolo and Toaripi.

sources.note: Phonology is given for Toaripi (8.15.1) and Orokolo (8.17.1) only. p.307 (Toaripi): 'Words of two or three syllables usually take the stress on the penultimate syllable... Where there are four or more syllables, there is a minor stress on the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress'; pronouns ara/are/ela/ere have final stress. p.350 (Orokolo): 'In stress, juncture, and intonation Orokolo is in agreement with Toaripi.' Keuru (Belepa) and Aheave are listed in Table 3 (p.295) as Western Eleman dialects; p.296: 'Their dialect [Aheave], like Keuru-Belepa and Muro, has close affinity…
